Propitiate

pro-PISH-ee-ate · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To propitiate is to win or regain the favor of someone.

For generations, the fishing village left the first catch of the season on the shrine to propitiate the sea before the real fishing began.

Worked Example

After the failed harvest, the council ordered extra offerings to propitiate the river spirit before anyone dared plant again.

The village believes the spirit's anger caused the bad harvest, so the offerings are meant specifically to win back its favor -- that is exactly what propitiate means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

appease: To appease is to calm an angry party by giving in to their demands -- peace bought by surrendering something they insisted on. To propitiate requires no demand at all: you offer gifts or gestures to win or keep the goodwill of a power whose anger would be dangerous.

conciliate: To conciliate is to win over the other side of an open dispute and bring the two of you back to agreement -- it works between quarreling equals. To propitiate runs one way, upward: a lesser party seeking the favor of a greater one whose displeasure could be dangerous.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

provoke: stir up anger deliberately

antagonize: cause hostility in

Where it sits · how far it goes to make amends — please → propitiate → atone

please vs. propitiate: To please someone is simply to make them happy; to propitiate them is to specifically win back their favor before their displeasure turns to anger.

atone vs. propitiate: Atone goes even further than propitiate, often implying a lasting effort to make up for a serious wrong, not just a single calming gesture.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — propiti

root — propiti: favorable (Latin (propitius))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: The root propiti- ('favorable,' from Latin propitius) plus the verb-forming -ate gives 'to make favorable' -- to propitiate someone is to win their favor before their displeasure turns to anger.

Use the root in a new word: propitious

Use the root in a new word: propitious: A propitious sign is a favorable one -- the same root as propitiate, just used to describe good timing instead of a calming gesture.

Root Check

Word Choice

Propitiate carries a formal, sometimes religious or ceremonial flavor -- appeasing a deity, a powerful authority, or someone whose anger could have serious consequences. For calming an ordinary person's everyday anger, mollify (this same unit) is the more natural choice.
